analysis.one_liner: Makes the lower tax rates on capital gains and dividends permanent.
analysis.headline: The bill to make the 2003 capital gains and dividend tax cuts permanent never got a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 tax law cut the tax rates on capital gains and dividend income, but those cuts were set to expire (a 'sunset') at the end of 2010. This bill would have deleted the expiration date, making the lower rates permanent. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who realize capital gains or receive taxable dividends — concentrated among the wealthiest households, plus money managers whose fees are tied to investment returns. A large share of the benefit would go to high-income filers, who hold most taxable capital gains and dividend income.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the expiration date in the 2003 tax law, so the reduced tax rates on capital gains and the taxation of dividends at capital gains rates would continue indefinitely instead of ending at the end of 2010 [S2] [S3].

Investors would keep the lower rates permanently rather than facing an announced future tax increase, reducing uncertainty about the after-tax return on selling appreciated assets or holding dividend-paying stock [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. Making the cuts permanent means forgoing the revenue that would have returned when they expired — a gap that must be filled by other taxes, borrowing, or smaller public spending.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the sunset permanently gives up federal revenue that was scheduled to return after 2010, adding to deficits or requiring other taxes or spending cuts to offset it [S2] [S3].

The benefit is concentrated at the top: taxable capital gains and large dividend income are held disproportionately by the wealthiest households, so the permanent rate cut functions mainly as a permanent tax reduction for high-income investors.

It widens the gap between how investment income and wage income are taxed, since the salary of a worker earning the same amount is taxed at ordinary rates while gains and qualified dividends get the lower rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — permanently lower taxes on investment income — flows mostly to households at the top of the income distribution, while the cost is a permanent revenue loss for the federal budget. Supporters argued lower rates encourage investment and that permanence ends uncertainty; opponents pointed to the revenue cost and the skew of the benefit toward the wealthy. The bill does nothing directly for wages, health care, or services that ordinary people rely on.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2007 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action on it, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Crapo introduced the bill on February 6, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
The bill would repeal the termination date in the 2003 tax law for the reduced individual capital gains rates and the taxation of dividends at capital gains rates [S2].
Forty-three senators cosponsored the bill, all Republicans [S4].
The only recorded action in the entire two-year Congress was the referral to Finance; the committee never acted on it, and it never received a vote in the Senate [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the scheduled expiration of the 2003 capital gains and dividend rate cuts remained on the books, and the federal budget retained the revenue those rates were set to bring in — while the high-income investors the bill would have helped permanently had to keep watching the sunset date.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal budget, not high-income investors

for.name: Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2003 capital gains and dividend rate cuts permanent

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it pending in committee

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote

sides.party_line_note: All 43 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support recorded; Democrats held the Senate majority and the Finance Committee chair, and the bill never moved after referral [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would lock in permanently the reduced tax rates on capital gains and dividends that were otherwise set to expire in 2010, preserving an after-tax advantage on investment income. The revenue given up is a cost borne by the broader federal budget.

industries.industry: Financial services industry (brokerages, funds, asset managers)
industries.note: Permanent lower rates on investment income support demand for investment products and after-tax returns, which the industry markets. The benefit comes at the price of federal revenue, not directly out of consumers' pockets.
